Include an ablation diagnostic: same added data volume as (B) but with non-redundant, informative auxiliary data (e.g., standard SVHN without redundancy) to check whether effects are due to added data/regularization rather than "covering". Budget fits by limiting to one architecture, 2-3 seeds, and leave-one-out approximations on only the sensitive subset.
decisive_metric: Primary: change in mean natural memorization score for the designated sensitive examples (Delta memorization = mean_memo_B - mean_memo_A), where memorization score is leave-one-out marginal utility (change in test loss/accuracy when the example is removed) or a consistent approximation thereof. Secondary mechanism check: correlation across sensitive examples between memo-score reduction and per-example membership inference confidence reduction; plus test accuracy difference to verify the claimed no-utility-loss aspect is not confounding the mechanism.
supporting_result: Over-memorization (B) yields a clear decrease in natural memorization scores for the sensitive subset versus baseline (A) while keeping test accuracy within ~0.5-1.0% of (A), and the per-example reductions in memorization scores significantly correlate with reductions in membership inference confidence/attack success; the non-redundant-data ablation does not produce the same memorization-score drop at matched data volume.
falsifying_result: Over-memorization (B) does not reduce (or increases) the sensitive subset's natural memorization scores relative to (A), or any membership inference improvement occurs without a corresponding drop in natural memorization (no correlation across examples), or the same effects are matched by the non-redundant-data ablation (indicating the method is just generic regularization/more-data), making the "covering via capacity redirection" mechanism not supported.

literature_gap: Two lines claim efficiency gains via ensembling/aggregation but for different failure models, and it is unclear if the efficiency mechanism transfers or conflicts: Multi-Dimensional Conformal Prediction (self-ensembled multi-head scores) reports smaller sets by better separating correct vs incorrect labels, while Reliable Prediction Sets (partitioned models + majority aggregation) and RSCP+ variants report robustness to poisoning/adversarial noise but note a tendency toward trivial full-label sets. The cross-paper tension is whether ensembling that improves separability (multi-dimensional scores) actually improves robust/reliable conformal under data poisoning, or whether robust aggregation inevitably collapses to large/trivial sets.
hypothesis: If we replace RPS's base nonconformity score with a multi-dimensional self-ensemble score (as in Multi-Dimensional Conformal Prediction), then under calibration-data poisoning the majority-aggregated prediction sets will stay reliable while becoming smaller, because multi-dimensional scores increase the margin between correct and incorrect labels, making each partition's conformal set less sensitive to poisoned calibration points and reducing the need to include many labels to maintain coverage.
minimal_test: On CIFAR-10 with a public open-weight backbone (e.g., ResNet-18 from torchvision, trained from scratch or using public weights), implement the published RPS pipeline for calibration-poisoning defense (split calibration into K subsets, build K conformal sets, majority aggregate). Compare two base scoring methods while keeping all RPS aggregation identical: (A) standard scalar nonconformity score used in RPS (baseline from ofuLWn8DFZ), (B) multi-dimensional nonconformity via multi-head self-ensembling on the same backbone as in loDppyW7e2. Attack: poison a fixed fraction p of the calibration set by flipping labels to a target class or random incorrect labels (run p in {0, 0.1, 0.2}). Also include an ablation/failure-mode diagnostic: vary head diversity by training identical heads (shared initialization, minimal diversity) vs diverse heads, to test whether any gain is from true multi-dimensional separation. Use a held-out clean test set for evaluating coverage and set size. Compute within <=8 A100 GPU-days by using a small backbone, modest epochs, and small K (e.g., K=5) and a single run per condition.
decisive_metric: Poisoning sensitivity curve of conditional coverage vs average set size: for each p, measure (1) empirical coverage on the clean test set (must be near 1-alpha), and (2) average prediction set size; summarize as area-under-curve of set size subject to meeting a minimum coverage threshold (e.g., coverage >= 1-alpha-0.01). Additionally, measure the mechanism directly: separation between correct and incorrect labels using the multi-dimensional score, e.g., the gap between the conformal score of the true label and the best competing label (median over test points), and how this gap degrades as p increases.
supporting_result: Across poisoning levels, the RPS+multi-dimensional variant maintains comparable coverage to baseline RPS (within 1 percentage point of 1-alpha) while yielding materially smaller sets (e.g., >=10-20% reduction in average set size at p=0.1 and p=0.2). The separation diagnostic shows a larger true-vs-best-wrong score gap for the multi-dimensional variant, and the advantage persists under poisoning; the diversity ablation removes most of the gain, indicating the effect is tied to multi-dimensional separation rather than incidental regularization.
falsifying_result: Under calibration poisoning, the multi-dimensional variant either (a) fails reliability by dropping coverage below baseline RPS by more than ~1-2 percentage points at the same alpha, or (b) achieves similar coverage only by producing equal or larger average set sizes than baseline RPS (no efficiency gain), or (c) shows no improvement in the separation diagnostic (true-vs-best-wrong gap similar to scalar baseline) and the diversity ablation changes nothing, suggesting the proposed mechanism does not transfer and the direction is not worth pursuing.

literature_gap: Motion Flow Matching claims ODE-style fast sampling and supports editing via trajectory rewriting, while MotionCLR claims fine-grained, word-level, training-free editing via cross-attention manipulation. The neighborhood lacks a mechanism-level check of whether fast flow-matching dynamics preserve localized text-motion editability, or whether low-step ODE sampling collapses word-aligned controllability compared to attention-based diffusion editing.
hypothesis: If low-step flow-matching sampling preserves local semantic controllability, then applying the same localized text edit (e.g., change only an action phrase) should produce a motion change temporally confined to the word-aligned segment with minimal spillover, comparable to MotionCLR, because the generative dynamics maintain a stable mapping between conditioning tokens and motion timesteps even under few-step integration.
minimal_test: On a public text-to-motion benchmark with paired captions (use KIT-ML as referenced by Motion Flow Matching), create a small set of minimal text edits on existing prompts (e.g., swap one verb phrase: walk->run; add/remove a modifier: with left hand wave; change count: two jumps). For each prompt, generate a baseline motion and an edited motion with (A) Motion Flow Matching (trajectory rewriting editing, 10-step sampling) and (B) MotionCLR (attention-map manipulation editing; use released/open weights if available, otherwise reproduce with open diffusion backbone per paper). Include one ablation diagnostic: run Motion Flow Matching at higher integration steps (e.g., 10 vs 50) to test whether edit localization depends on step count. Keep seeds fixed per method for before/after comparisons.
decisive_metric: Edit localization vs spillover: compute (1) temporal change localization score by aligning baseline and edited motions in time and measuring the fraction of total joint-position change energy that falls inside the predicted word-aligned time window (for MotionCLR use its cross-attention peak window; for Motion Flow Matching use a heuristic window from action timing estimated by a pretrained motion-text aligner such as a public CLIP-like motion-text model, applied identically across methods), and (2) semantic success for the edited phrase using a pretrained action classifier on motion (public, e.g., HumanAct12/UESTC-trained) evaluated only on the edited segment. Report localization-energy fraction and segment-level action accuracy delta.
supporting_result: Motion Flow Matching achieves segment-level semantic success comparable to MotionCLR (e.g., within 5-10% absolute in segment action accuracy for the edited phrase) while maintaining high localization (e.g., >=0.7 of change energy inside the target window) and low spillover outside the window, and the 10-step vs 50-step ablation shows similar localization, indicating few-step sampling does not degrade word-level editability.
falsifying_result: Motion Flow Matching edits either fail semantically on the target phrase (small or negative segment action accuracy delta) or produce diffuse changes (e.g., localization-energy fraction <=0.4 with substantial off-window changes) while MotionCLR remains localized, and/or Motion Flow Matching only becomes localized at much higher step counts (large improvement from 10 to 50), implying the fast ODE sampling/editing direction is not worth pursuing for fine-grained text-aligned editing.

literature_gap: Invariance Starvation claims spurious reliance can disappear simply by scaling more IID data (same spurious proportion) once the invariant function is representable, while EvA and LaSAR posit that spurious reliance is encoded in specific activation channels/neurons and can be removed post hoc by erasing/blocking them. It is unclear whether the gains of activation-level erasure are actually targeting stable spurious mechanisms versus just reweighting features that would naturally vanish with more data; none of the activation methods are directly tested across a controlled data-scaling axis where spurious proportion is held fixed, creating a cross-paper mechanism ambiguity.
hypothesis: If spurious reliance under ERM is primarily due to invariance starvation (insufficient data to encode invariant features), then increasing training set size while keeping spurious proportion fixed should (a) reduce spurious-feature encoding in internal activations and (b) shrink the marginal benefit of post-hoc activation erasure (EvA/LaSAR), because the model no longer needs explicit channel/neuronal suppression once invariant features are learned.
minimal_test: On a public spurious benchmark with known group splits (e.g., Waterbirds with background as spurious attribute), train the same open-weight architecture from scratch with ERM at 3 training-set sizes (e.g., 10%, 30%, 100% of the original training set) using stratified subsampling that preserves the spurious correlation rate. For each trained checkpoint: (1) evaluate vanilla ERM; (2) apply EvA as the post-hoc baseline from the supplied papers; (3) include an ablation diagnostic by applying EvA with randomly permuted spurious-indicator scores across channels (same sparsity/erasure budget) to test whether EvA is using meaningful spurious channels. Keep compute minimal by using a single standard backbone (e.g., ResNet-50) and one seed per setting if needed, staying within <=8 A100 GPU-days.
decisive_metric: Data-scaling curve of (i) worst-group accuracy (minority group) and (ii) the EvA improvement delta over ERM (worst-group accuracy after EvA minus before) across training sizes, plus a mechanism diagnostic: correlation between EvA-identified channels and a spurious-attribute linear probe accuracy from the penultimate layer (high probe accuracy implies spurious information present). The key decisive quantity is whether EvA delta and spurious-probe signal both monotonically decrease with more data at fixed spurious rate, and whether the random-score EvA ablation fails to produce the same improvement.
supporting_result: As training size increases, ERM worst-group accuracy rises while (a) spurious-attribute probe accuracy from embeddings decreases and (b) EvA’s added benefit over ERM shrinks toward ~0 at the largest data setting; additionally, EvA with random-permuted scores yields near-zero or significantly smaller gains than true EvA, indicating EvA is only helpful when genuine spurious channels exist (mostly at small-data settings).
falsifying_result: Even at the largest training size (with spurious proportion preserved), spurious-attribute probe accuracy remains high and EvA continues to deliver a substantial worst-group accuracy gain comparable to the small-data setting, or the random-score EvA ablation produces similar gains to true EvA. Either outcome would weaken the invariance-starvation explanation as the primary driver and suggest activation-level erasure is not merely compensating for limited data (or is not specifically targeting spurious mechanisms).

literature_gap: Two strands address different structure assumptions but are not cross-evaluated: (1) structure-aware hierarchical/conditional BO via explicit conditional embeddings and attention-based deep-kernel GP (An Attention-based Approach for BO with Dependencies) and (2) structure-agnostic “everything as strings” LM embedding regression for BO (Predicting from Strings). It is unclear whether the LM-string approach actually captures conditional-activation dependencies that hierarchical BO methods target, or whether it degrades specifically on conditional spaces where explicit structure should help.
hypothesis: If we encode the same hierarchical conditional configuration space as strings and use Embed-then-Regress, its surrogate will show systematically worse conditional generalization than a structure-aware conditional surrogate, because generic LM embeddings do not reliably represent parent-child activation constraints and conditional parameter relevance.
minimal_test: On a public tree-structured conditional BO benchmark used in hierarchical BO settings (use the tree-structured simulation benchmark from the dependencies/conditional-space paper if publicly released; otherwise use a standard public conditional HPO benchmark like ConfigSpace/HPOLib-style hierarchical spaces), run BO for a fixed small budget (e.g., 10 random init + 40 BO steps) with identical acquisition (EI) and identical evaluation oracle. Compare three surrogates: (A) structure-aware conditional surrogate from “An Attention-based Approach for BO with Dependencies” (their embedding + attention deep-kernel GP), (B) Embed-then-Regress from “Predicting from Strings” using an open-weight LM to embed stringified configurations then a regressor/GP head, and (C) an ablation baseline: the same string pipeline but with parent activation indicators explicitly appended as tokens (e.g., “ACTIVE:child_branch=1/0”) to test whether failures are specifically about conditional structure encoding rather than general modeling capacity. Keep wall-clock compute within <=8 A100 GPU-days by using a small open model for embeddings and caching embeddings for all queried configs.
decisive_metric: Conditional generalization error diagnostic, not just best-found value: after each BO iteration, evaluate the surrogate on a held-out set of configurations stratified by conditional branches and activation patterns, and report (i) branch-conditioned NLL (or RMSE) per branch, and (ii) calibration of predictive uncertainty under activation switches measured as the average absolute error in predicted improvement when flipping a parent choice that activates/deactivates a subtree (counterfactual activation test). Also report standard BO simple regret curve as secondary.
supporting_result: Across seeds, method (A) achieves lower branch-conditioned NLL/RMSE and better counterfactual activation calibration than (B), while (C) closes some of the gap relative to (B). This pattern indicates the key missing piece for (B) is encoding conditional activation structure, validating the value of explicit hierarchical/conditional modeling.
falsifying_result: Embed-then-Regress (B) matches or outperforms (A) on branch-conditioned NLL/RMSE and counterfactual activation calibration (not only on simple regret), and adding explicit activation tokens (C) provides no consistent improvement. This would weaken the claim that explicit structure-aware conditional surrogates are necessary, suggesting the string/LM embedding approach already captures the relevant dependency mechanism well enough.

literature_gap: Two mechanistic papers claim safety is concentrated in tiny, identifiable self-attention components (single “safety heads” via Ships/Sahara; <1% “safety neurons” mostly in self-attention layers via SN-Tune), but the VL-adaptation paper reports safety degrades during vision-language adaptation even with safe data, implying those safety components may not be preserved or may stop controlling outputs after adaptation. It is unclear whether VL adaptation specifically disrupts these safety heads/neurons (mechanism) versus shifting behavior for other reasons (e.g., decoding/prompting or distribution shift).
hypothesis: If vision-language adaptation degrades safety by disrupting the pre-adaptation safety-critical attention circuitry, then the safety heads/neuron set identified on the base LLM should lose their measured safety importance after VL adaptation, and ablating the pre-identified components should have a smaller marginal harmfulness increase in the adapted model because they are already less functional.
minimal_test: Use an open-weight LLM with a public VL-adapted counterpart (as in the VL-adaptation paper’s setting; e.g., LLaMA-family base vs an open LVLM derived from it). Step 1: On the base chat/instruct model, identify top-K safety heads using Ships/Sahara (from “Attention Heads” paper) and independently identify a safety-neuron mask using the detection method from SN-Tune. Step 2: Transfer the same head indices and neuron mask to the VL-adapted model (same backbone layers). Step 3: Evaluate harmful-query refusal/safety on a public harmful prompt set (same prompt set for both models) under four conditions for each model: (a) no ablation, (b) ablate top-K safety heads, (c) ablate random K heads matched by layer, (d) zero out the SN-Tune safety neuron mask vs a size-matched random neuron mask. Include MSSBench text-only queries (ignore images) as an out-of-distribution safety set to see whether effects generalize beyond the harmful prompt set used for identification.
decisive_metric: Mechanism-linked marginal safety drop: DeltaH = (harmful-success rate or harmfulness score)ablated - (harmful-success rate or harmfulness score)clean, computed separately for targeted vs random ablations, and compared between base and VL-adapted models. Also track preservation of importance rankings: Spearman correlation between head importance scores (Ships) computed on base vs VL-adapted for the shared backbone heads.
supporting_result: VL-adapted model shows (1) significantly lower base-to-adapted rank correlation of Ships head-importance (near 0) and/or reduced importance mass concentrated in the original top-K, and (2) reduced targeted-vs-random ablation gap: in the base model, targeted ablation causes a much larger DeltaH than random ablation, but in the VL-adapted model targeted ablation yields little extra DeltaH over random (or overall DeltaH is already high), consistent with those safety components being disrupted by adaptation.
falsifying_result: Importance and causal effect are preserved: Ships head-importance rankings remain similar pre/post adaptation (high Spearman correlation), and targeted ablation continues to cause a substantially larger DeltaH than random ablation in the VL-adapted model (comparable to the base model). This would suggest VL adaptation safety degradation is not primarily due to loss of the identified safety head/neuron circuitry, weakening the direction of focusing on preserving these specific components during adaptation.

literature_gap: FairGI claims to jointly achieve group fairness and an individual-fairness-within-groups notion via a similarity matrix plus adversarial group-fairness training, while Individual Fairness as an Extension of Group Fairness argues individual fairness requires randomized (probabilistic) predictions and questions an inherent trade-off; neither is checked in a standardized in-processing benchmark setting (FFB) with an explicit determinism-vs-randomization ablation to see whether randomization is actually necessary for improving individual fairness without harming group fairness.
hypothesis: If we add controlled prediction randomization at inference time to an in-processing group-fairness-trained classifier, individual fairness (pairwise consistency under a similarity metric) will improve without systematically worsening group fairness, because probabilistic outputs reduce discontinuities that deterministic classifiers create at decision boundaries.
minimal_test: Using one tabular dataset already supported by FFB (e.g., Adult/Census Income) and one standard in-processing baseline from FFB (e.g., an adversarial debiasing or fairness-regularized classifier), train the model as in FFB. Then compare three inference variants on the same trained model: (A) deterministic thresholding at 0.5, (B) randomized thresholding by sampling Bernoulli(p) from the predicted probability p for each example, and (C) calibrated-temperature sampling (p_T from temperature-scaled logits, then Bernoulli(p_T)) with T tuned on a validation split to match overall positive rate of (A). Include a failure-mode diagnostic by stratifying all metrics by margin-to-threshold (examples with p near 0.5 vs far), since the mechanism predicts effects should concentrate near the boundary.
decisive_metric: Change in an individual-fairness metric computed from a similarity graph on features (e.g., kNN in standardized feature space): average absolute difference in predicted positive probability between each point and its k nearest neighbors, reported overall and stratified by margin-to-threshold; alongside standard group-fairness gaps used in FFB (statistical parity difference and equal opportunity difference) to detect any induced group-level degradation.
supporting_result: Compared to deterministic inference (A), randomized variants (B) and/or (C) show a statistically meaningful reduction in neighbor prediction-discrepancy (overall and especially for near-threshold points), while keeping statistical parity and equal opportunity gaps within a small tolerance band of (A) (e.g., no consistent worsening across seeds, and changes smaller than the fairness improvements).
falsifying_result: Randomization (B)/(C) does not reduce the neighbor prediction-discrepancy (or only reduces it trivially while increasing it for far-from-threshold points), or it systematically worsens statistical parity/equal opportunity gaps relative to (A) across seeds, indicating that probabilistic predictions are not a practical lever for improving individual fairness without harming group fairness in the FFB in-processing setting.

literature_gap: BLSP claims behavior alignment (same LLM generation given speech vs transcript) via a lightweight adapter trained on LLM-generated continuations, but its advantage is unclear. In tension, end-to-end systems (Spectron, LLaMA-Omni) claim stronger spoken QA/interaction quality and knowledge retention, yet rely on heavier training and less accessible components/data. The missing decisive evaluation across these directions is whether BLSP-style behavior alignment actually improves downstream instruction/QA under realistic speech perturbations (where end-to-end models are often evaluated) rather than only matching text continuations.
hypothesis: If we train a BLSP-style lightweight speech-to-LLM adapter using continuation-writing distillation from transcripts, then under speech noise/ASR-like corruptions the model should preserve transcript-conditioned answer behavior better than a direct-initialization baseline, because the adapter is explicitly optimized to make speech-conditioned hidden states induce the same next-token distribution as transcript-conditioned states.
minimal_test: Use an open LLM (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Llama-2-7B-chat) frozen + open speech encoder (e.g., Whisper encoder or wav2vec2) frozen. Train (<=8 A100 GPU-days) a small modality adapter with BLSP-style two-step: (1) for each sample, prompt the LLM with the transcript prefix and sample a continuation/answer; (2) train the adapter to reproduce those targets given the speech input. Compare to baseline: direct initialization adapter trained only to predict the ground-truth transcript tokens from speech (ASR-style) then feed transcripts to the LLM (cascaded) OR a randomly initialized adapter trained on the same targets without the transcript-prefix continuation step (ablation). Evaluate on a public spoken QA set with paired audio+text, e.g., Spoken SQuAD (or the spoken subset of Natural Questions if available publicly), plus a stress condition by adding standard noise/reverb (MUSAN/RIR) to audio at multiple SNRs.
decisive_metric: Behavior-consistency under perturbation: for each question, compute (a) KL divergence between the LLM next-token distributions when conditioned on transcript vs conditioned on speech (averaged over the answer generation steps), and (b) answer invariance rate: percentage of samples where the speech-conditioned answer matches the transcript-conditioned answer up to normalization (exact match or token-level F1), reported as a function of SNR. Also report a failure-mode diagnostic: cases where ASR WER is low but answer invariance is low (indicating modality misalignment rather than recognition errors).
supporting_result: Across SNR levels, the BLSP-trained adapter shows substantially lower transcript-vs-speech KL and higher answer invariance than the direct-init/ASR-style baseline, especially in the low-to-moderate noise regime where WER is similar across methods, and the remaining failures correlate with genuine transcript ambiguity rather than systematic modality drift.
falsifying_result: BLSP-trained adapter does not reduce transcript-vs-speech KL or improve answer invariance compared to the baseline/ablation (or only improves when WER improves), and the mismatch remains high even when the transcript is correctly recognized (low WER), implying behavior alignment via continuation distillation is not the limiting factor and the approach is not worth pursuing for downstream spoken QA/interaction robustness.

literature_gap: Across structure-aware PLMs, there is a tension between (a) methods that inject structure into an existing sequence PLM via parameter-efficient adapters (MULAN) and report only limited gains at large model sizes, and (b) methods that more heavily modify attention or retrain on large structure databases (PST, ProteiNexus) claiming broad improvements. The gap is that none of these papers isolates whether structural supervision actually adds new structural information beyond what a strong sequence PLM already encodes, versus merely acting as an auxiliary training signal whose marginal benefit vanishes when the base PLM is large.
hypothesis: If explicit structural inputs (angles/distances) provide genuinely new information beyond sequence-only pretraining, then on proteins where structure is perturbed while sequence is held constant, a structure-aware model (e.g., MULAN) should track the perturbed structure in its representations/predictions more than a sequence-only baseline (ESM-2), because the structure pathway is causally used rather than being redundant.
minimal_test: Use a public protein structure dataset with multiple experimentally determined conformations for the same (or near-identical) sequence (e.g., PDB entries for the same UniProt with different liganded states). Construct pairs (seq, struct_A) and (same seq, struct_B). Run two frozen encoders: (1) ESM-2 (sequence-only baseline from PST/MULAN comparisons), (2) MULAN (sequence+structure adapter). For each pair, measure how much the embedding changes when swapping struct_A vs struct_B while keeping sequence identical. As an ablation/failure-mode diagnostic for MULAN, feed the correct sequence with a mismatched structure from a different protein of similar length (structure-shuffle) and measure whether the embedding changes spuriously. Keep compute minimal: no training, just forward passes over ~5k paired examples; optionally repeat on two MULAN sizes to mirror the 'limited on large PLM' claim.
decisive_metric: Structure-sensitivity ratio: for each model, compute delta_within = mean cosine distance between embeddings of (seq, struct_A) vs (seq, struct_B) for same sequence; and delta_mismatch = mean cosine distance between (seq, correct_struct) vs (seq, shuffled_struct). Report (i) delta_within for MULAN vs ESM-2, and (ii) delta_mismatch/delta_within for MULAN as the failure-mode diagnostic (should be >1 if mismatched structures cause larger, detectable perturbations than real conformational changes).
supporting_result: MULAN shows substantially larger delta_within than ESM-2 (e.g., >=2x) indicating embeddings respond to true structural variation at fixed sequence, and the ablation shows delta_mismatch >> delta_within (e.g., ratio >=2), indicating the structure channel is actively used and can detect incorrect structural conditioning rather than being ignored.
falsifying_result: MULAN delta_within is similar to ESM-2 (e.g., <10% relative increase) or near zero, implying structure input is largely redundant/ignored; and/or delta_mismatch is not larger than delta_within (ratio ~1), implying the model does not meaningfully condition on structure or cannot distinguish mismatched structures, making heavier structure-injection directions less compelling.

literature_gap: DIOTM claims displacement interpolation across time improves stability and OT-map approximation, but reviewers note a potential theoretical gap from restricted parameterization of t-dependent maps. In tension, Not-So-Optimal Transport Flows argues that making trajectories closer to OT (straightening) can make early-time dynamics harder to learn and hurt scalability, motivating intentionally non-optimal/hybrid couplings. It is unclear whether DI-style multi-time supervision actually makes early-time dynamics easier (as implied by stability claims) or harder (as implied by trajectory-straightening difficulty), and this mechanism is not directly evaluated.
hypothesis: If DIOTM-style multi-time displacement-interpolation supervision truly stabilizes learning because it provides consistent gradients across t, then (compared to single-time OT-map training) it should reduce early-time gradient/trajectory pathology (e.g., exploding/oscillatory updates and high curvature/acceleration of predicted paths).
minimal_test: On a small unpaired image-to-image translation setting used by OT-map methods (e.g., two domains from a public dataset such as CelebA attribute split or a standard translation benchmark), train (A) a baseline neural OT-map method from the DIOTM paper that uses max-min/single-t training and (B) DIOTM with multi-t displacement interpolation supervision, matching network size, optimizer, and compute. Add one ablation (C) DIOTM but with a restricted t-parameterization variant (the suspected theoretical-gap setting) or with only two t points (early+late) instead of the full trajectory. For each run, log per-iteration discriminator/dual objective, generator/map loss, and compute path diagnostics by sampling x and evaluating predicted maps at multiple t to estimate discrete-time velocity and acceleration along the learned trajectory.
decisive_metric: Early-time (small t) trajectory learnability/stability diagnostics: (1) gradient-norm distribution and spike rate (fraction of steps where gradient norm exceeds a fixed multiple of its running median) for the map network, and (2) discrete acceleration magnitude along the predicted interpolation path, computed as mean over samples of ||T(t+dt,x) - 2T(t,x) + T(t-dt,x)||/dt^2 for small t. Secondary: training-instability rate measured as number of divergent runs across 5 seeds under a fixed hyperparameter setting.
supporting_result: Compared to baseline (A), DIOTM (B) shows materially fewer gradient spikes and lower early-time discrete acceleration (smoother/easier-to-fit early trajectory) while also reducing divergent runs across seeds; the ablation (C) partially loses these improvements, linking the effect to multi-time supervision and/or adequate t-parameterization.
falsifying_result: DIOTM (B) has similar or worse early-time gradient spike rate and similar or higher early-time discrete acceleration than baseline (A), and does not reduce divergent runs across seeds; additionally, ablation (C) behaves similarly to (B), indicating the claimed stability does not come from the displacement-interpolation trajectory supervision/parameterization and the direction is not worth pursuing for this mechanism.

literature_gap: eoB6JmdmVf finds speech language models’ alignment to higher-level language regions largely disappears once low-level speech/text features are removed, suggesting weak brain-relevant semantics; KL8Sm4xRn7 claims brain-tuning both increases alignment in semantic language regions and reduces reliance on low-level speech features. The unresolved tension is whether brain-tuning truly increases feature-invariant (semantic) brain alignment, or whether gains come from residual/alternative low-level cues or evaluation leakage on the same stimulus properties.
hypothesis: If brain-tuning genuinely injects brain-relevant semantics into speech models, then after explicitly removing low-level stimulus features from model representations (as in eoB6JmdmVf), the brain-tuned model should retain substantially more alignment to semantic language ROIs than the untuned baseline, because the tuned representation carries more feature-invariant semantic information that predicts late-language cortex activity.
minimal_test: Using the same public naturalistic story fMRI dataset/protocol as eoB6JmdmVf (read vs listened to the same stories), take one open-weight speech LM family used in KL8Sm4xRn7 (or reproduce their released brain-tuned checkpoint). For each condition (listening; optionally reading for cross-modal generalization), compute voxelwise encoding (or RSA) to fMRI in predefined ROIs: early auditory and semantic language regions. Run the eoB6JmdmVf intervention: regress out/eliminate low-level stimulus features from the model representations (their textual/speech feature removal procedure) and recompute alignment. Compare four settings: (1) baseline speech LM, raw reps; (2) baseline, feature-removed reps; (3) brain-tuned, raw; (4) brain-tuned, feature-removed. Include an ablation diagnostic: repeat feature removal with an intentionally over-aggressive setting (e.g., higher-rank regression / stronger projection) to verify both models degrade similarly in early auditory ROIs (sanity check that removal actually targets low-level cues).
decisive_metric: In semantic language ROIs, the retained-alignment ratio under feature removal: (alignment_feature_removed / alignment_raw), compared between brain-tuned and baseline, evaluated out-of-story via cross-validation; plus the differential retention between semantic ROIs and early auditory ROIs (semantic retention minus auditory retention) to ensure the effect is not general noise-robustness.
supporting_result: Brain-tuned model shows a clearly higher retained-alignment ratio than baseline specifically in semantic language ROIs (e.g., baseline collapses as in eoB6JmdmVf while brain-tuned retains a substantial fraction of raw alignment), while both models show strong drops in early auditory ROIs after feature removal (sanity). The semantic-minus-auditory retention gap is larger for brain-tuned than baseline.
falsifying_result: After feature removal, brain-tuned and baseline speech models lose a similar fraction of alignment in semantic language ROIs (no meaningful increase in retained-alignment ratio for brain-tuned), or any retention advantage appears equally (or more) in early auditory ROIs, implying improvements are not due to increased brain-relevant semantics and the direction is not worth pursuing on this mechanism.

literature_gap: There is a cross-paper tension about what representation actually enables LLM usefulness for time series: LLM-ABBA claims symbolizing time series into existing LLM tokens effectively bridges to downstream numeric tasks, while Can LLMs Understand Time Series Anomalies? finds LLMs work better when time series are presented as images than as text/tokens and that explicit reasoning prompts do not help. It is unclear whether ABBA-tokenization provides any genuine advantage for anomaly detection beyond being a convenient discretization, or whether the key is visual/shape encoding rather than token semantics.
hypothesis: If ABBA tokenization genuinely transfers salient time-series structure into the LLM token space (rather than relying on generic pattern cues), then an LLM operating on ABBA tokens should outperform the same LLM operating on a length-matched naive discretization (e.g., uniform binning into tokens) for subtle anomaly detection, because ABBA preserves amplitude-and-period patterns that are critical for detecting non-trivial anomalies.
minimal_test: On a public time-series anomaly detection dataset used by Can LLMs Understand Time Series Anomalies? (or an equivalent public benchmark they evaluate), create two text encodings per series: (A) ABBA tokenization as in LLM-ABBA; (B) a control tokenization with identical sequence length and vocabulary size produced by uniform quantization/binning of values (or random codebook) so that only ABBA's structure-preserving property differs. Use the same open-weight LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct or similar) in the same few-shot setup for both encodings, with identical prompts and shot selection. Include one baseline from the anomaly paper: the image-based representation prompting of the same LLM. Add one failure-mode diagnostic ablation: shuffle the ABBA token order within each series while keeping the token histogram fixed, to test whether performance depends on temporal structure vs token frequency cues.
decisive_metric: Change in anomaly localization quality attributable to structure preservation: segment-level (or point-level) anomaly F1 (or AUPRC) computed over anomaly intervals, and the delta between ABBA vs uniform-binning at matched token length; plus the drop in F1/AUPRC under the ABBA token-order shuffle (structure ablation).
supporting_result: ABBA-token LLM achieves a statistically meaningful improvement over uniform-binned token LLM on subtle/non-trivial anomalies (e.g., higher interval-F1/AUPRC), and its performance drops markedly when ABBA token order is shuffled (showing reliance on temporal structure). Image-based prompting may still be best overall, but ABBA should clearly beat the matched naive-token control if its claimed mechanism matters.
falsifying_result: ABBA-token LLM performs no better than (or worse than) the length/vocab-matched uniform-binned token control, and/or ABBA performance is unchanged under token-order shuffling (indicating reliance on token frequency or prompt artifacts rather than preserved temporal structure). In that case, pursuing ABBA-style token bridging for anomaly detection would be weakened relative to image/shape-based representations.

literature_gap: There is a cross-paper tension between (i) LACR-style graph recovery from natural language via associational relation extraction plus constraint-based pruning, which implicitly leans on faithfulness (noted as a weak point under text co-occurrence), and (ii) the claim that full graph recovery is not necessary because causal order alone can suffice for effect estimation. It is unclear whether extracting only a causal order from text is actually more robust than extracting edges when language induces systematic faithfulness violations, and whether any robustness translates to downstream causal effect accuracy rather than just graph-structure scores.
hypothesis: If we replace LLM-extracted edge graphs (LACR-style) with LLM-elicited causal order (order-only) for downstream causal effect estimation, then effect estimates will be less sensitive to spurious text co-occurrence (faithfulness violations) because ordering queries require less reliance on correlational language patterns than edge existence claims.
minimal_test: Use a public synthetic causal text benchmark with known ground-truth graph and effects (Cladder, as used/mentioned in the counterfactual-from-text work). Create two text conditions for the same underlying SCM: (A) original item text, (B) a minimally edited version that injects a strong but non-causal co-occurrence cue (e.g., repeated phrases linking two non-adjacent variables, or a confounding-sounding sentence) while keeping the ground-truth SCM and queried causal effect identical. For each item, run (1) an open-weight LLM to extract edges then prune with a constraint-based method as in the LACR paradigm, and estimate the target effect via backdoor adjustment using the recovered graph; (2) the same open-weight LLM to elicit a topological order (pairwise order queries aggregated to a total order as in the order-based paper), then estimate the same effect using an order-only identification procedure (e.g., choose adjustment sets consistent with the order, or compute effect via ordered factorization / selecting parents consistent with order). Include an ablation diagnostic: for the order-only pipeline, replace the LLM-elicited order with a random order matched in size to quantify how much effect accuracy depends on meaningful ordering vs chance. Budget: one 7B-13B open model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or similar open-weight) with deterministic decoding; evaluate on a small fixed subset (e.g., 300-500 items) to fit <=8 A100 GPU-days.
decisive_metric: Faithfulness-sensitivity of downstream causal effect estimation: delta-effect-error = mean absolute error of estimated causal effect (vs ground-truth effect from the SCM) under condition B minus condition A, computed separately for the edge-graph pipeline and the order-only pipeline. Also report the direction-of-effect flip rate between A and B (percentage of items where the sign of the estimated effect changes while the true sign does not) as a failure-mode diagnostic directly tied to spurious textual association.
supporting_result: Order-only shows substantially smaller delta-effect-error and lower flip rate than edge-graph recovery (e.g., edge pipeline degrades markedly under spurious co-occurrence edits while order-only remains near its A-condition performance), and the random-order ablation performs near chance/worse, indicating the robustness comes from meaningful elicited order rather than an artifact of the estimator.
falsifying_result: Order-only has similar or larger delta-effect-error (and/or flip rate) than edge-graph recovery under the spurious co-occurrence edits, or both pipelines degrade similarly; additionally, if the random-order ablation matches the LLM-elicited order performance, it would indicate the order signal is not doing causal work, weakening the premise that order elicitation is a more robust alternative worth pursuing.

literature_gap: Instruction Following without Instruction Tuning suggests instruction-following can emerge from shifting the response distribution (even via rule-based logit tweaks), while Do LLMs know internally when they follow instructions? finds an internal instruction-following dimension that generalizes across tasks but not across instruction types and appears tied to prompt phrasing. It is unresolved whether response-distribution-only adaptations actually create instruction-type-robust compliance or merely improve compliance for a narrow set of phrasing patterns, which would align with the non-generalization across instruction types. This mechanism-level tension is not checked with a fine-grained instruction-following benchmark like the knowledge-task instruction benchmark that separates task correctness from instruction compliance.
hypothesis: If response-distribution-only adaptations mainly act as a phrasing-sensitive compliance heuristic (rather than learning instruction semantics), then on the knowledge-task instruction benchmark they will show strong dependence on instruction type/phrasing (large variance in compliance across instruction templates) and their improvements will be predictable from (and potentially controllable by) the instruction-following internal dimension, rather than from task difficulty.
minimal_test: Use an open-weight base LM used in Instruction Following without Instruction Tuning (or a close open equivalent) and create three model variants: (A) base model, (B) response-only finetuned model (responses without instructions) as in that paper, and (C) the paper’s rule-based adapter (end-of-sequence probability ramp + repetition penalty + fixed 15-word logit shifts) applied at inference. Evaluate all three zero-shot on the knowledge-task instruction-following benchmark (qit4pa6PpY) with at least two distinct instruction types/templates from the benchmark (e.g., conditional-on-correctness vs option-space-modifying instructions) plus the benchmark’s distractor instructions. Additionally, for each evaluated prompt, compute the instruction-following-dimension score from qIN5VDdEOr (fit the linear direction on a small public dev split using model (A) only, then apply to all models without refitting), and test whether failures cluster by instruction type and correlate with the dimension score. Baselines: model (A) and instruction-tuned/open chat baseline if available from qit4pa6PpY results for the same backbone family; failure-mode diagnostic/ablation: compare (B) vs (C) and also shuffle the instruction text (keep task identical) to isolate phrasing effects.
decisive_metric: Primary: instruction compliance rate conditioned on task correctness, reported separately by instruction type/template and by distractor vs non-distractor conditions (not just overall accuracy). Mechanism diagnostic: correlation (e.g., AUROC) of the instruction-following-dimension score with per-example compliance, computed separately for each instruction type, plus the change in compliance when the instruction text is paraphrased/shuffled while keeping the task constant.
supporting_result: Models (B) and/or (C) improve average compliance over (A) but show large drops for at least one unseen instruction type/template (high between-template variance), and compliance is strongly predictable from the instruction-following-dimension score within each template; shuffling/paraphrasing the instruction causes substantial compliance changes without comparable changes in task correctness. This would support that response-distribution shifts mainly yield phrasing-sensitive instruction-following consistent with qIN5VDdEOr’s non-generalization across instruction types.
falsifying_result: Response-only finetuning (B) yields consistent compliance gains over (A) across all tested instruction types/templates with low between-template variance, weak dependence of compliance on the instruction-following-dimension score (near-chance AUROC), and minimal sensitivity to instruction paraphrase/shuffle when task content is fixed. This would weaken the claim that response-distribution-only methods primarily act via prompt-phrasing heuristics and suggest they may improve instruction-type-robust instruction semantics, making the “phrasing-limited” mechanism unlikely.

literature_gap: DRDO claims robustness to noisy/non-deterministic preference labels by explicitly modeling rewards + a novel preference likelihood, while DICE shows self-bootstrapping using DPO implicit rewards can strongly improve alignment but relies on synthetic preferences produced by the current policy. It is unclear whether DRDO’s robustness advantage holds in the specific bootstrapping regime where preference noise is endogenous (self-generated, potentially mode-collapsing), or whether it behaves like (or worse than) standard DPO when the preference data are produced by the model itself.
hypothesis: If we replace DICE’s inner-loop DPO update with DRDO on the same self-generated preference data, then training will exhibit less degeneracy (e.g., reduced reward hacking/length bias and fewer collapsed preference margins) because DRDO’s joint reward-distillation + preference-likelihood formulation is more robust to noisy or low-confidence pair labels than Bradley-Terry DPO.
minimal_test: Run 2-round bootstrapping on an open-weight base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct or Mistral-7B-Instruct) using the DICE recipe to generate a synthetic preference dataset from the model’s own implicit reward on UltraFeedback prompts (public). Compare two update rules for the same generated dataset and compute budget: (A) DICE baseline (DPO with DICE’s length-regularized reward shaping + replay) vs (B) DRDO substituted for DPO (keeping the same data generation, shaping, and replay). Include an ablation diagnostic: repeat (A) and (B) with DICE length-regularization turned off to stress-test length/reward hacking. Keep total training to <=2 bootstrap rounds and small batch/steps to fit <=8 A100 GPU-days.
decisive_metric: Degeneracy/robustness diagnostic on the self-generated preference dataset: measure preference-margin collapse and length bias of the learned implicit reward. Concretely: (1) margin distribution: mean and lower-tail (e.g., 10th percentile) of r(theta, y_w) - r(theta, y_l) on a held-out set of generated pairs; (2) length-reward correlation: Spearman correlation between implicit reward and response length on held-out prompts; (3) self-consistency flip rate under paraphrase: fraction of prompt paraphrases where the preferred output (per implicit reward) changes for the same two candidate responses. These directly test whether the method is robust to endogenous noisy labels and avoids reward/length hacking.
supporting_result: Compared to DICE(DPO), DRDO-in-DICE yields (i) higher lower-tail reward margins (fewer near-zero/negative margins), (ii) significantly lower reward-length correlation especially when length regularization is off, and (iii) lower paraphrase flip rate, while maintaining similar average implicit-reward improvement over rounds.
falsifying_result: DRDO-in-DICE shows no improvement or worse outcomes on the robustness diagnostics—e.g., similar or more margin collapse, equal or higher reward-length correlation (especially in the no-length-regularization ablation), and no reduction in paraphrase flip rate—indicating DRDO’s claimed noise robustness does not transfer to the self-bootstrapping/implicit-reward regime and is not worth pursuing for this direction.

literature_gap: A cross-paper mechanism mismatch: FJD claims jailbreak prompts are detectable via first-token confidence under a manual instruction (distributional shift), but h4rm3l/AutoDAN/Prompt-Translation explicitly optimize and re-express jailbreaks to look benign (low perplexity, human-readable, compositional transformations). It is unclear whether FJD detects the attacker intent (prompt-level) or only correlates with downstream harmfulness, and whether it is robust to compositional/translated attacks that preserve semantics while matching benign-looking surface form.
hypothesis: If FJD is primarily picking up surface-form distribution shift (rather than attacker intent), then jailbreaks produced by compositional transformations (h4rm3l) and translated-to-coherent attacks (prompt translation / AutoDAN-style interpretable suffixes) will reduce the FJD detection signal (first-token confidence gap) while keeping attack success rate high, because these attacks explicitly make prompts look benign/readable and bypass simple filters.
minimal_test: Use one open-weight aligned chat model as victim (e.g., Llama-2-Chat-7B or Vicuna-7B) and a small harmful instruction set from a public red-teaming dataset (e.g., AdvBench or HarmBench prompts). Create three prompt sets of equal size: (A) benign user requests matched by length/topic; (B) baseline jailbreak prompts from AutoDAN (or a public GCG/AutoDAN prompt set if available) targeting the victim; (C) compositional/rewritten jailbreak variants built by applying a limited h4rm3l-like subset of string-transform primitives (e.g., roleplay framing, quoting/translation wrapper, instruction obfuscation, delimiter games) to the same harmful requests, plus a 'coherent translation' rewrite (human-written or small open model rewrite) that keeps semantics but improves readability. Run FJD on all prompts (no extra victim queries beyond what FJD needs). Separately, measure attack success by querying the victim once per prompt and scoring with a public harmfulness classifier baseline (or a simple keyword/regex policy for a narrow category) plus spot-checking a small sample for calibration. Include an ablation diagnostic: remove the FJD manual instruction prefix and re-run FJD to confirm the claimed mechanism depends on it.
decisive_metric: Primary: separation of FJD score distributions between benign (A) and each jailbreak set (B,C), measured as AUROC and the mean first-token logit margin (or confidence) gap. Mechanism diagnostic: change in FJD separability (delta AUROC and delta mean margin) from (B) to (C) at matched attack success rate; plus the ablation effect size when removing the manual instruction (drop in AUROC).
supporting_result: Compared to baseline AutoDAN/GCG-style jailbreaks (B), the compositional/translated jailbreaks (C) maintain similar attack success (e.g., within 5-10 percentage points) but substantially reduce FJD detectability (e.g., AUROC drops from >0.8 on B to ~0.6-0.7 on C, and the first-token confidence gap vs benign shrinks markedly). Removing the FJD manual instruction causes a large degradation in separability, consistent with a surface-form distribution-shift mechanism.
falsifying_result: FJD remains strongly separative for (C) despite the attacks being more benign-looking/readable (e.g., AUROC stays high and close to that for B, and the first-token confidence gap remains large), or (C) only reduces FJD detectability by also collapsing attack success (i.e., detectability decreases only when the jailbreak no longer works). Either outcome would weaken the claim that compositional/translated jailbreaks can evade near-free detection by neutralizing surface-form distribution shifts.

literature_gap: Across papers there is a tension between (a) training-free, grounding/attention-based methods claiming temporally consistent multi-attribute edits (Ground-A-Video) and (b) training-based paired-data methods claiming improved long-video consistency via sampling corrections (Consistent Video-to-Video Transfer). Neither line cleanly isolates whether consistency gains come from the proposed mechanism (cross-frame gated attention vs long-video sampling correction) or simply from reduced edit strength, and reviewer notes highlight difficulty assessing temporal consistency (e.g., missing/insufficient video results in PDEdit and RACCooN). A minimal mechanism-specific check is missing: does each method actually reduce temporal flicker at fixed edit accuracy on the same prompts/videos?
hypothesis: If cross-frame gated attention is the primary driver of temporal consistency in training-free multi-attribute video editing, then enabling it (vs removing it) in a Ground-A-Video-style pipeline will reduce frame-to-frame temporal artifacts at the same level of edit correctness; if instead consistency mainly comes from sampling corrections/smoothing (as emphasized by Consistent Video-to-Video Transfer), then attention gating removal will not significantly increase flicker once sampling correction/smoothing is held constant.
minimal_test: Run a controlled ablation on a small public benchmark: select 30 short clips (8-16 frames) from DAVIS-2017 or YouTube-VOS validation (public) and define 2 multi-attribute text edit prompts per clip (e.g., change object color + add accessory; or change background style + remove small object) with a fixed template. Use an open-weight text-to-image diffusion backbone used by Ground-A-Video (or closest open equivalent) and implement the Ground-A-Video pipeline twice: (1) full method with cross-frame gated attention; (2) identical pipeline but cross-frame gated attention disabled (replace with per-frame attention or ungated aggregation), keeping all other components identical (modulated cross-attention, optical-flow inverted-latent smoothing, same seeds, same number of diffusion steps). Include one baseline from the supplied papers: Ground-A-Video full method as the baseline system, and the ablation as the failure-mode diagnostic. Budget fits by limiting to 60 edits total and low step counts.
decisive_metric: Temporal consistency at fixed edit success: (a) compute optical-flow-warping error on non-edited background regions (lower is better) using RAFT (open weights) flow between consecutive frames, warp frame t to t+1 and measure LPIPS or L1 residual outside the automatically inferred edited region; (b) edit correctness per prompt using an open VLM (e.g., CLIP or a small open VLM) scoring whether the target attributes appear, plus a simple object-preservation check (DINOv2 feature cosine similarity on unchanged regions). Report a consistency-vs-edit-correctness tradeoff curve across a small sweep of guidance scales; the key diagnostic is whether gating shifts the curve (better consistency for same correctness).
supporting_result: Across guidance scales, the full cross-frame gated attention variant achieves clearly lower background warping residual (e.g., >10-15% relative reduction in flow-warp LPIPS/L1) at matched edit-correctness (within a small tolerance, e.g., ±2% on the VLM attribute score), and the ungated variant shows a characteristic failure mode: localized flicker or drifting changes in frames where attributes are not supposed to change.
falsifying_result: Disabling cross-frame gated attention yields no meaningful degradation in the consistency-vs-correctness curve (e.g., <3-5% relative change in flow-warp residual at matched edit-correctness), or any apparent consistency gain from gating is explained by reduced edit correctness (the gated method only looks more consistent because it under-edits). This would weaken the claim that gated attention is the decisive mechanism worth pursuing versus sampling/smoothing-driven consistency.

literature_gap: Across papers, there is a tension between (a) approaches that claim improved 3D consistency by injecting explicit 3D feedback into a pretrained 2D/multi-view diffusion sampler (3D-Adapter) and (b) approaches that claim improved 3D quality by coupling 2D and 3D diffusion priors (BiDiff) or reframing 3D as multi-view 2D with cross-view attention (ZERO-1-to-G). None of these abstracts/reviews make clear whether the claimed geometry gains come from the specific 3D-aware mechanism (3D feedback augmentation / bidirectional guidance / cross-view attention) versus generic extra compute or iterative self-conditioning, and the neighborhood lacks a mechanism-targeted diagnostic that isolates multi-view geometric consistency from texture quality.
hypothesis: If explicit 3D feedback in the denoising loop is the main cause of improved geometric consistency (as claimed by 3D-Adapter), then adding 3D-Adapter-style feedback to a fixed multi-view diffusion baseline (MVDream or Zero123++ as referenced by 3D-Adapter) should reduce cross-view 3D inconsistency at equal sampling budget more than a compute-matched control that uses no 3D reconstruction/rendering, because the 3D reconstruction enforces a shared latent 3D structure across views rather than only correlating 2D features.
minimal_test: Use a public multi-view dataset with ground-truth camera poses and mesh/pointcloud such as Objaverse subset or a small GSO-like open subset (any publicly available set with renders + camera parameters). For N=200 prompts/objects, generate 6-view image sets with (1) baseline multi-view diffusion (MVDream, accepted) and (2) the same baseline augmented with 3D-Adapter fast feed-forward (Gaussian splat) feedback during sampling (as in 3D-Adapter). Add one compute-matched control: baseline with extra denoising steps or feature self-conditioning so wall-clock matches the 3D-Adapter run but without 3D decode-render-encode. Reconstruct a 3D representation from each generated 6-view set using the same public reconstruction method for all conditions (e.g., DUSt3R/MASt3R-style multi-view depth+pose if open weights, or a standard Gaussian-splat optimization initialized from views), keeping reconstruction settings fixed. Report metrics per object and aggregate.
decisive_metric: Multi-view geometric inconsistency measured directly from the generated views using the known/estimated cameras: (a) depth reprojection error: predict per-view depth from the reconstructed 3D, reproject into other views, and compute mean absolute depth disagreement on visible pixels; and (b) cycle-consistency photometric error under reprojection (warp view i into j using reconstructed geometry and compare to generated view j) restricted to non-occluded pixels. Also report a failure-mode diagnostic: proportion of samples with high inconsistency (e.g., top-10% depth reprojection error) to capture catastrophic geometry collapse.
supporting_result: Compared to both the baseline and the compute-matched control, the 3D-Adapter-augmented sampler shows a clear reduction in depth reprojection error and reprojection photometric error (e.g., >10-15% relative drop) and a lower rate of catastrophic inconsistency outliers, while image-level perceptual quality (optional sanity check via CLIP score or aesthetic score) stays roughly similar, indicating the improvement is specifically geometric rather than just quality/compute.
falsifying_result: 3D-Adapter augmentation does not improve (or worsens) depth reprojection and cycle-consistency errors relative to the compute-matched control, or any gains are fully explained by extra sampling compute (compute-matched control matches the improvement). Additionally, if the outlier failure rate is unchanged, this would weaken the claim that explicit 3D feedback is the key mechanism worth pursuing for consistency.
